Systematic mapping studies classify the primary literature and reveal publication trends and research gaps, but conducting one manually is slow and error-prone. The data extraction and mapping step consumes the greatest share of researchers' effort while attracting the least automation, existing work having concentrated upon study selection.

This study designed, developed and evaluated a machine learning pipeline that automates the data-extraction-and-mapping phase. The pipeline is unsupervised throughout and consumes no annotated labels at any stage. It ingests full-text papers, recovers descriptive metadata and body structure from publisher PDFs, assigns each paper to the research-type, contribution-type and evaluation-method facets by comparing it with natural-language descriptions of the published category definitions, induces thematic categories through transformer embeddings and clustering, and assembles a classified portfolio and visual map. Every assignment carries a confidence margin, and low-margin assignments are flagged for human review.

Applied to the behaviour-driven development corpus of Binamungu and Maro (2023), the pipeline processed 123 of 126 documents and produced a complete map in 46.4 seconds, against a published estimate of 107 minutes per study for manual extraction. Because no annotated corpus was available, the evaluation establishes internal consistency and aggregate correspondence rather than per-paper accuracy. Facet distributions correspond to the published manual mapping with benchmark scores between 0.869 and 0.938, reproducing the ordering of categories but not their relative sizes. A classifier trained on the pipeline's own assignments recovers them with macro-averaged F1 between 0.484 and 0.513, and per-class results identify categories that cannot be recovered at all. Assignments flagged for review are recovered substantially less often than unflagged ones, confirming that the confidence margin is informative.

The study contributes a reproducible unsupervised pipeline that converts full-text publications into structured mapping data without labelled training material, together with evidence that semantic representation decisively outperforms lexical representation and that the fidelity of PDF text extraction governs every downstream result. Feasibility is demonstrated; accuracy is not, and establishing it requires a hand-annotated sample, which the pipeline prepares on every run.

Secondary studies synthesise existing primary studies rather than collecting new data, providing structured and reliable summaries of what is already known in a research area. Several types of secondary studies exist, including systematic literature reviews (SLRs), meta-analyses, and systematic mapping studies (SMSs). An SLR aims to identify relevant primary papers, extract the required data, and synthesise the results to answer specific research questions in depth, following a strict protocol that covers search strategy, selection criteria, and quality assessment. A meta-analysis statistically combines results from primary studies to produce generalisable evidence expressed as effect sizes and confidence intervals.

A systematic mapping study, by contrast, is a methodology used to identify, categorise, and analyse a research topic by examining the quantity and type of research conducted and by revealing the gaps and opportunities in that area

. It aims to provide an overview of a research field, and its expected outcome is a classified portfolio of publications that identifies the quantity of research, the available results, and the publication trends within the field
. In effect, an SMS offers a map-like visual summary of a research area, which is why mapping studies have become common across software engineering, medicine, pharmacy, and healthcare
Conducting an SMS involves five steps: the definition of research questions, the search for relevant studies, the screening of papers, keywording using abstracts, and data extraction and mapping

. Each step contributes to the rigour and traceability of the final map, but the steps differ substantially in the human effort they demand. The fifth step, data extraction and mapping, is widely regarded as the most crucial and the most costly, because data are read from each paper, classified against a scheme and recorded in tables from which statistics and visual maps are produced.
The distinction between these secondary study types matters for what automation must achieve. An SLR seeks to answer narrow questions by deeply synthesising outcome data, so automating it

requires extracting fine-grained, study-specific results. An SMS instead seeks breadth, classifying many studies along a small number of categorical facets to chart a field. The data an SMS extracts are therefore largely categorical and structurally regular, which makes it a more tractable and more rewarding target for machine learning: the same classification scheme applies across the whole corpus, and success can be measured by agreement with documented expert labels.

The growth of the scientific literature compounds the need for such automation. As the number of published primary studies in software engineering continues to rise, the manual effort required to map a field grows in proportion, and the window during which a map remains current shrinks. A method that reduces the per-study cost of extraction therefore does more than save time on a single study; it changes what is feasible, making it practical to construct larger maps and to keep them up to date as the literature evolves.
1.1.1 The Challenges of Conducting an SMS Manually

Conducting a systematic mapping study manually poses several well-documented challenges, chief among them tediousness, error-proneness and difficulty of updating. Systematically reviewing and categorising a large body of literature is labour-intensive, and the volume of information makes manual processes susceptible to oversights. Among the five steps, data extraction is the most time-consuming, because data are extracted by hand and recorded in tables, and because the number of articles included in a secondary study can range from dozens to thousands. Full automation is difficult owing to the different ways researchers report results, restricted full-text access and the incomplete information supplied by some authors.

Empirical evidence underscores the cost of manual extraction. Felizardo et al. (2024) report that, on average, a researcher spends 107 minutes per study, and that dual-independent data extraction takes up to 172 minutes per study; they further note that data extraction bias can undermine the validity of evidence synthesis, with error rates reaching as high as 63%. Nussbaumer-Streit et al. (2021) similarly found that extracting major information on study design, participants and results took one person an average of 41 to 65 minutes per study. At the level of the whole study, Petersen et al. (2015) observe that a manual systematic mapping study can take up to 67 weeks from inception to completion. Beyond the initial effort, keeping a secondary study up to date as the literature evolves is itself a recurring burden

With the rise of machine learning and artificial intelligence, the literature has emphasised the use of these technologies in systematic literature reviews, where the inclusion and exclusion of papers (screening) have received considerable attention (Van Dinter et al., 2021; Marshall & Wallace, 2019). However, the most labour-intensive steps, namely data extraction and synthesis, remain understudied (Aliyu et al., 2018), and most research on automating reviews targets systematic literature reviews rather than systematic mapping studies. Three gaps are especially consequential for the present work.

First, the absence of a unified extraction framework. Jonnalagadda et al. (2015) found that no unified data-extraction framework focused on secondary studies existed, that prior work addressed only a handful of data elements, and that the absence of common manually annotated reference sets made cross-study comparison impossible.

Second, limited handling of heterogeneous publication metadata. Existing tools tend to target a small, fixed set of clinical fields and struggle with the heterogeneous metadata research type, contribution type, evaluation method, and thematic focus that mapping studies actually require

Third, most extraction tools are confined to the biomedical domain and to screening, and rarely produce the SMS-specific outputs evidence maps, bubble plots and gap charts that mapping studies depend upon
1.1.3 Contribution and Positioning of This Study

Recognising these gaps, the present study focuses on using machine learning to automate the data extraction and mapping step of the systematic mapping process. It designs, develops and evaluates a pipeline that ingests full-text papers, extracts descriptive metadata, assigns each paper to the established mapping facets, induces thematic categories, assembles the classified portfolio and visual map, and evaluates every step against the published classification of a manually conducted mapping study.

Current tools fall short in three specific ways that this study addresses directly. They offer no unified framework that links metadata extraction to facet classification and to map generation; this study provides exactly such an end-to-end framework. They handle only a narrow, fixed set of

fields and falter on the heterogeneous metadata of mapping studies; this study targets the full set of facets that constitute a software-engineering map and treats thematic categorisation as a first-class, data-driven component. And they are validated almost exclusively on biomedical screening rather than software-engineering mapping; this study is developed and evaluated against published software-engineering mapping studies used as manually annotated reference sets. In short, where existing work automates the easiest step of the wrong study type in the wrong domain, this study automates the hardest step of the right study type in the domain where the methodology originated.

Conducting a systematic mapping study requires meticulous searching, screening, and data extraction across academic databases, conference proceedings, and journals, followed by the careful extraction and categorisation of relevant data from each paper by research type, theme, contribution, and evaluation method. Given the volume of papers and the detail of the analysis, the process is resource-intensive and prone to human error. Manual data extraction and categorisation can introduce inconsistencies and missed information that undermine the reliability of a study’s findings, while the time required can delay completion to the point where the map is outdated before it is published; manual mapping studies have been reported to take up to 67 weeks to complete (Petersen et al., 2015).

Automation of the data-extraction phase could substantially reduce this effort. Marshall and Wallace (2019) show that combining machine learning with natural language processing can automate the extraction of relevant information from research papers, improving consistency and reducing errors. Despite this promise, no widely adopted, reproducible pipeline currently targets the data extraction and mapping step of systematic mapping studies, links it to a unified set of metadata features, and produces the SMS-specific outputs that mapping studies need.

To make the problem measurable, the study evaluates the pipeline against two reference points. Effectiveness is measured as agreement with the manually assigned labels of the reference mapping study of Binamungu and Maro (2023), reported per paper (accuracy, precision, recall, and macro- and micro-averaged F1 for each facet) and at the level of the map from the reference mapping study by Binamungu and Maro (2023). Efficiency is measured as the wall-clock time the
pipeline needs per study, set against the manual baseline of 107 minutes per study for a single reviewer and 172 minutes for dual independent extraction reported by Felizardo et al. (2024).
The main objective of this study is to design, develop, and evaluate a machine learning pipeline to automate the data extraction and mapping phase of systematic mapping studies.
The specific objectives of the study are:
i. To identify a unified set of publication-metadata features required to extract and map data in a systematic mapping study.
ii. To collect and preprocess a corpus of full-text academic papers, recovering from publisher PDFs the descriptive metadata and body structure upon which automated extraction depends.
iii. To design and implement an unsupervised machine learning pipeline capable of automating the extraction and mapping process from full-text academic papers without labelled training data.
iv. To evaluate the pipeline against a manually conducted mapping study of the same field, in terms of the correspondence of its output, its internal consistency, and the effort it requires.
Corresponding to the specific objectives, the study answers the following questions:
i. Which unified set of publication-metadata features can be used to extract and map data in a systematic mapping study?
ii. How can a corpus of full-text academic papers be collected and preprocessed so that descriptive metadata and body structure are recovered reliably enough to support automated extraction?

iii. How can an end-to-end unsupervised machine learning pipeline be designed and implemented to extract mapping data and induce thematic categories from full-text papers without labelled training data?
iv. To what extent does the output of such a pipeline correspond to a manually conducted mapping study, and what effort does it require by comparison?

The adoption of machine learning in systematic mapping studies has the potential to improve the data extraction and thematic mapping steps significantly. This research aims to create a pipeline that not only expedites the SMS process but also enhances the quality and reliability of the resulting maps.

First, the study contributes to the automation of systematic mapping studies, making them more efficient and less dependent on scarce expert time. Second, the pipeline can accelerate knowledge synthesis across domains, enabling researchers to keep maps current with reduced effort. Third, by producing a reproducible and openly described pipeline together with an annotated dataset, the study provides reusable resources that other researchers can adopt or extend, strengthening methodological rigour in evidence-based software engineering and supporting capacity-building in research-synthesis tooling in low-resource settings.

The significance can be made concrete by considering who benefits and how. For the individual researcher or postgraduate student, the mechanical part of the most labour-intensive phase of a mapping study is reduced from minutes per paper to seconds, freeing effort for the judgement calls that remain. For research groups that maintain living maps, the same reduction makes periodic updating feasible. For the broader discipline, a transparent and reproducible pipeline, accompanied by a manually annotated dataset derived from a peer-reviewed mapping study, lowers the barrier to comparing and improving automation methods. These benefits are pursued without displacing expert judgement: the design keeps a human reviewer in control of low-confidence decisions, and the evaluation reports candidly where automation still falls short of the experts.

Although a systematic mapping study comprises several steps, this study focuses specifically on the data extraction and mapping step. The pipeline therefore begins with a set of relevant papers for which inclusion and exclusion criteria have already been applied; the search and screening steps are outside its scope. Because mapping studies differ by topic, the study uses an existing, manually conducted mapping study as its manually annotated baseline for developing and evaluating the models. The work is situated within the software-engineering domain, and the behaviour-driven-development mapping study of Binamungu and Maro (2023), whose primary studies and published
per-paper classifications constitute the corpus and the ground truth, serves as the reference baseline.

2.2 Systematic Mapping Studies and Publication Characteristics
2.2.1 Secondary Studies and the Place of the SMS

Secondary studies analyse, summarise or synthesise existing research rather than collecting new data. The most commonly adopted variants are the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and the Systematic Mapping Study (SMS). The primary goal of an SLR is to answer specific research questions in depth by synthesising evidence through detailed analysis
, whereas the primary goal of an SMS is to provide an overview of a broad research area, classify studies and identify gaps or trends

. The two differ in granularity and intent: an SLR drills down, while an SMS spreads out to chart the shape of a field. This difference matters for automation, because the data an SMS extracts are largely categorical metadata used to position each study on a map, rather than the fine-grained outcome data an SLR synthesises.

The distinction also shapes what success means for automation. Because an SMS applies one classification scheme across an entire corpus, an automated SMS can be judged by its agreement with documented expert labels, study by study and facet by facet. This makes the SMS a well-posed machine learning target: the categories are defined in advance, the ground truth exists in
published mapping studies, and the evaluation reduces to measuring agreement, which is the basis of the methodology adopted in Chapter Three.

According to Petersen et al. (2015), an SMS proceeds through the five steps as shown in Figure 1. The first step defines the research questions, delimiting the scope of the review. The second step applies a search string derived from the questions to the title, abstract, and keywords of candidate papers. The third step screens papers against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The fourth step is keyword extraction in the abstracts: reviewers identify keywords and concepts that capture each paper’s contribution, then combine them into a classification scheme that becomes the blueprint of the map.

The fifth step, data extraction and mapping, is the focus of this study. Here, researchers read each paper in full, classify it using the scheme, store the extracted information in data sheets, compute statistics, and build visual maps. The systematic mapping guidelines treat this step not merely as a procedure but as a quality-critical activity: data extraction typically uses structured forms that capture metadata such as research type, contribution, method, venue, and thematic focus, and a dual-reviewer approach is often employed in which one researcher extracts data and another validates it (Kitchenham et al., 2010), to mitigate bias and enhance descriptive validity.

Mapping, or classification, uses both topic-independent and topic-specific schemes. Topic-independent classifications include research type, research method, and publication type, and are often grounded in established frameworks that support cross-study comparison. Topic-specific classifications are either drawn from existing taxonomies, such as SWEBOK, or developed

inductively through keywording and open coding. The guidelines also highlight inconsistency in classification when the same scheme is applied by different researchers, underlining the need for clear definitions, training, and consensus, and they make use of visual tools such as bubble plots, heat maps, and bar charts to represent categorised results intuitively.
2.2.3 The Nature of Publication Metadata in Systematic Mapping Studies

This subsection examines the nature of metadata that mapping studies actually extract. Understanding the structure of publication metadata is essential because it determines which natural language processing and machine learning techniques are appropriate for automating extraction.

Publication metadata in a mapping study falls into two broad groups. The first group is descriptive bibliographic metadata that is available directly from the document or its catalogue record: title, abstract, author keywords, publication year, authorship, venue, and publication type. This metadata is comparatively structured and is frequently obtainable through parsing and pattern matching, because it occupies predictable positions in the document and follows recognisable surface patterns. The second group is analytical, map-defining metadata that does not appear verbatim in the paper and must instead be inferred from the text: research type, contribution type, evaluation method, and thematic category of the study. This second group is what makes mapping studies hard to automate, because it requires reading comprehension rather than pattern matching.
The map-defining facets are well established in software engineering. The research-type facet, derived from

classification, distinguishes solution proposals, validation research, evaluation research, experience reports, and opinion or philosophical papers; it captures the maturity of a contribution and the extent to which it has been evaluated. The contribution-type facet distinguishes the kind of artefact a study delivers: tools, methods, processes, models, or metrics. The evaluation-method facet records how a contribution was assessed, for example, discussion, rigorous analysis, simulation, case study, or experiment, indicating the strength of its empirical grounding. The thematic facet captures the sub-topics of the field and is usually induced from the corpus through keywording. These facets are largely categorical and mutually structured, which is precisely why supervised classification and topic modelling are natural automation tools for them.

Three properties of this metadata shape the design of any automation pipeline. It is heterogeneous, spanning structured bibliographic fields and inferred analytical categories that demand different techniques. It is imbalanced, because some categories (for example, solution proposals) dominate while others (for example, opinion papers) are rare, which is why evaluation must weight categories fairly. The process is partly latent, as the thematic categories are not predefined but instead emerge from the underlying corpus. This characteristic motivates the integration of an unsupervised, embedding-based component alongside supervised classification algorithms. The pipeline in this study is structured around exactly these three properties.
2.2.4 Data Extraction and Mapping as the Principal Bottleneck

The evidence reviewed establishes that data extraction constitutes the most resource-intensive and least automated stage of secondary studies. The study by Büchter et al. (2020) confirms, through a scoping review of methodological guidance, that data extraction remains largely manual and reliant on spreadsheets and human judgement, that existing recommendations are fragmented and often insufficient for less-experienced reviewers, and that comprehensive tools to automate this step are still lacking. Therefore, the combination of high cost, high error rate, low automation, and weak tooling makes the data extraction and mapping step the natural target for the present study.
2.2.5 Evidence-Based Software Engineering and the Role of Maps

Systematic mapping studies sit within the broader programme of evidence-based software engineering, which seeks to integrate the best available research evidence with practical experience and human values when making decisions about software development and maintenance. Within this programme, secondary studies provide the mechanism by which scattered primary findings are aggregated into actionable knowledge. Mapping studies, in particular, perform an agenda-setting function: by revealing which questions have been heavily studied and which remain open, they guide the allocation of future research effort and help practitioners locate the evidence relevant to a decision. This function is only as reliable as the extraction and classification underlying it, which is why the quality, consistency and timeliness of the data extraction and mapping step are central to the value of the whole enterprise.
Because a map is a living description of a field, its usefulness decays as new primary studies appear. Keeping a map current therefore requires repeating the data extraction and mapping step

periodically, multiplying the manual cost. The notion of a living systematic review, in which evidence is continually incorporated, has gained traction in other disciplines, and its feasibility depends squarely on reducing the per-study cost of extraction. Automation of the kind pursued in this study is thus a precondition for living maps in software engineering, not merely a convenience.
2.3 Automation Efforts in Systematic Mapping and Review

Much of the research on automating secondary studies has concentrated on screening, that is, identifying relevant studies from large corpora. Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. (2020) developed a machine learning pipeline that integrates active learning to prioritise studies for human annotation, reducing screening effort by over 85%. Tools such as ASReview enable semi-automated screening using probabilistic classifiers and user feedback. To reduce labelling requirements, active-learning techniques incorporating uncertainty sampling, diversity-based selection and intelligent stopping criteria have become common, and document embeddings from models such as BERT and Sentence-BERT have improved classifier performance with fewer labelled examples. These systems demonstrate that machine learning can sharply reduce manual labour in initial filtering; however, they are largely confined to relevance classification and have limited impact on the downstream tasks specific to mapping.

Data-extraction automation is less mature. Van Dinter et al. (2021), reviewing 41 primary studies on SLR automation, found that although automation is common in study selection, only five reviewed studies addressed data-extraction automation, typically using full-text documents and classification algorithms, and identified the translation of domain models into machine-readable formats as a key challenge. Jonnalagadda et al. (2015) reviewed automatic extraction of critical data elements from full-text medical texts, identifying 52 potential data elements drawn from standard resources such as the Cochrane Handbook, the CONSORT statement and the PICO and PIBOSO frameworks; they concluded that no unified extraction framework existed, that prior work addressed only one to seven elements at a time, and that the absence of common manually annotated reference sets prevented direct comparison. Bui et al. (2016) built an extractive summarisation system that highlights key clinical elements such as sample size and PICO values, using SVM-based sentence
ranking and ontology-based knowledge representation, and they found that the optimal model varies by data type, underscoring the need for tailored rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

Automated extraction tools such as RobotReviewer, which is strong for risk-of-bias assessment, and ExaCT, which focuses on trial characteristics, have been applied successfully in clinical domains. However, their utility in mapping studies remains underexplored. Sundaram and Berleant (2023) identify a persistent gap in tools capable of automatically extracting structured metadata (research methods, outcomes and populations) across heterogeneous studies, and note that mapping studies additionally require topic clustering, trend visualisation and domain-specific taxonomies that existing tools rarely address. Tsou et al. (2020) compared the screening-prioritisation performance of Abstrackr and EPPI-Reviewer and found both useful for reducing screening workload; these tools, like Rayyan, support collaborative screening and tagging but are not designed to produce SMS-specific outputs such as evidence maps or gap-analysis charts. De La Torre-López et al. (2023) similarly observe that AI-based extraction has been explored mainly through ontology-based systems and SVM classifiers, and that scarcity of tools, simplistic feature representations, domain-specific retraining requirements and a lack of reproducibility benchmarks continue to limit maturity.

Wewerka and Reichert (2023), analysing 63 publications on robotic process automation, reinforce the boundary of rule-based automation: RPA suits rule-based, repetitive tasks over structured data but cannot handle the interpretive, unstructured nature of complex extraction such as that found in secondary studies, and integrating AI with RPA to handle semi-structured data remains at a prototype stage. Taken together, the existing tool landscape indicates that the analytical, map-defining metadata of systematic mapping studies remains the aspect least adequately addressed by current automation tools.
2.3.4 Automation of Review Updating and AI-Assisted Reviews

Beyond screening and extraction, researchers have begun to automate the continual updating of evidence syntheses. Chernikova et al. (2024) demonstrate machine-learning-assisted continuous updating of a meta-analysis in an educational context, showing that classifiers can flag newly relevant studies for inclusion as they are published, keeping a synthesis current with bounded

human effort. Wagner et al. (2022) take a wider view, examining how artificial intelligence is reshaping the conduct of literature reviews across their full lifecycle; they argue that AI is most mature in the mechanical stages of search and screening and least mature in the interpretive stages of extraction and synthesis, precisely the imbalance this study addresses. These contributions show a field moving from automating the easy, mechanical steps towards automating the hard, interpretive ones, and they locate the present study at that frontier.
2.3.5 Critical Synthesis of the Automation Literature
Read together, the automation literature exhibits three recurring limitations that frame the present study. First, a phase imbalance:

effort has concentrated on study selection, where the task reduces to a single binary include/exclude decision, while data extraction, which requires recovering many heterogeneous fields and assigning several analytical facets, has received far less attention and is rarely evaluated as a complete system (Van Dinter et al., 2021; Marshall & Wallace, 2019). Second, a domain skew:

the extraction systems that do exist were developed largely for clinical evidence, where reporting is comparatively standardised, and they transfer poorly to software-engineering mapping studies, whose publication metadata and facet schemes differ markedly (Jonnalagadda et al., 2015).

many contributions are proofs of concept reported on small or idiosyncratic corpora without shared baselines, which makes results difficult to compare or reproduce (Felizardo et al., 2024). These three limitations phase imbalance, domain skew, and the evaluation gap are not independent; together they explain why no unified, reproducible extraction-and-mapping pipeline for software-engineering mapping studies yet exists, and they motivate the manually annotated, macro-aware, end-to-end design pursued in this study. The specific gaps that follow from this synthesis are stated formally in Section 2.6.
2.4 Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing Techniques

The preceding sections reviewed what has been automated and how well. This section provides the technical foundation by explaining the core machine learning and natural language processing techniques that are relevant to automating data extraction and mapping. The aim is to demonstrate the methodological understanding that underpins the design choices in Chapters Three and Four, rather than merely to report applications from the literature.

Assigning each paper to a research type, contribution type, and evaluation method is a multi-class text-classification problem, for which supervised learning is the natural approach. A supervised classifier learns a mapping from a feature representation of a document to a categorical label, using a set of labelled training examples. Several families of classifiers are relevant. Support Vector Machine (SVM) finds the hyperplane that maximally separates classes in a high-dimensional feature space and, with appropriate kernels and regularisation, performs strongly on sparse, high-dimensional text features. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) classifiers optimise a linear model (for example, a hinge or logistic loss) by iterating over training examples; they scale well to large, sparse datasets and often match SVMs on text while training faster. Tree-based ensembles such as random forests and gradient-boosted trees combine many decision trees to capture non-linear interactions and provide feature-importance estimates, although they can be less effective than linear models on very high-dimensional sparse text. Multinomial Naïve Bayes provides a fast probabilistic baseline that models class-conditional word frequencies. Allam et al. (2025), surveying text-classification research from 2019 to 2024, report that contextual deep-learning representations consistently outperform classical algorithms, while also noting persistent challenges of overfitting, class imbalance, and computational cost considerations that motivate combining classical classifiers with modern embeddings rather than discarding either.

A brief intuition clarifies why particular classifiers suit this task. A support vector machine seeks the decision boundary that leaves the widest possible margin between classes; on text, where documents are points in a very high-dimensional term space, such margin-maximising boundaries generalise well and resist overfitting. A stochastic-gradient-descent classifier learns a similar linear boundary but updates its parameters one example at a time, which makes it fast and memory-frugal on large sparse matrices while retaining the strengths of linear models. Logistic regression outputs calibrated class probabilities, which is convenient for the confidence thresholding used in the human-in-the-loop mode. Random forests aggregate many decision trees trained on random subsets of features and examples, capturing non-linear interactions at the cost of higher sensitivity to dimensionality. Multinomial Naïve Bayes assumes conditional independence of terms given the
class and, despite this strong assumption, provides a fast and surprisingly competitive baseline. The empirical comparison in Chapter Five tests these intuitions on the actual corpus.

The transformer architecture introduced the self-attention mechanism, which weighs the relevance of every token to every other token in a sequence and thereby captures long-range context. BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a transformer encoder pre-trained on large corpora using masked-language-modelling and next-sentence objectives; it produces contextual representations in which the same word receives different vectors depending on its surroundings. Sentence-BERT (SBERT) adapts BERT with a Siamese training objective so that whole sentences or passages can be embedded efficiently and compared by cosine similarity, which makes it well suited to document-level clustering and retrieval. Transformer encoders are central to this study in two ways: they supply the sentence embeddings that represent each study for the thematic component and, where available, for the classifiers, and they underlie the class-based descriptors of the topic model. Their main costs, computational demand and the need for sufficient data, are mitigated here by using pre-trained models and by combining them with lighter classical components

Thematic categories in a mapping study are latent and must be induced from the corpus, which is the province of topic modelling. Classical Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) models each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words; it is interpretable but relies on bag-of-words features and can struggle with short or specialised texts. Embedding-based topic modelling, exemplified by BERTopic, instead embeds documents with a transformer, reduces the dimensionality of those embeddings (for example, with UMAP), clusters them, and derives interpretable topic descriptors with a class-based TF–IDF weighting. The clustering step can be density-based (HDBSCAN), which discovers the number of themes and flags outliers, or centroid-based (k-means), in which the number of clusters k is chosen by an internal validity index such as the silhouette coefficient, the mean over documents of how much closer each document is to its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster. Weißer et al. (2020) demonstrate the value of clustering for topic filtering within secondary studies, supporting the choice of an embedding-and-clustering approach for the thematic component of the pipeline.

Most directly relevant to this study, Felizardo et al. (2024) present a proof-of-concept that uses a large language model for data extraction in a software-engineering systematic mapping study. Their results indicate that automated extraction can approach manual quality for several facets while drastically reducing effort, but they report variability across data elements and caution that the approach requires careful evaluation against manual baselines. Zhao et al. (2021) provide a large-scale mapping study of natural language processing for requirements engineering, analysing 404 primary studies from 1983 to 2019; this work is doubly relevant because it exemplifies the kind of large mapping study whose extraction burden motivates automation and because it illustrates the classification facets an automated pipeline must reproduce. The present study builds on this direction by constructing a complete, reproducible pipeline that combines metadata feature extraction, supervised facet classification and transformer-based topic modelling, and by evaluating it against a manually conducted mapping study used as a manually annotated reference set. A recurring theme across the reviewed literature is the tension between generality and specificity. General tools are reusable but shallow, handling only fields common to many study types; specific tools are deep but brittle, requiring retraining for each new domain. The design adopted here seeks a middle path: a general pipeline architecture whose components are specialised to the software-engineering mapping task through a domain-specific annotated corpus, so that the architecture is reusable while the trained models are accurate for the target domain. The existing tools can be arranged along two dimensions: the review stage they automate and the domain they target. The overwhelming majority occupy the screening-and-biomedical region; very few address extraction in software engineering, and fewer still produce map-specific outputs. The present study deliberately occupies that sparsely populated region and adds the map-generation capability that even its nearest neighbours lack.

Although the automation of systematic reviews has seen substantial advances in automating systematic literature reviews (SLR), the specific requirements of systematic mapping, such as thematic categorization, visual summaries, and comprehensive data extraction and mapping, are still inadequately addressed. This study aims to address this gap by employing a machine-learning approach to automate data extraction, a crucial step in the systematic mapping study process. This automation is expected to reduce errors and effort and minimize the time required to carry out the SMS process, making it more efficient. The goal is to gather unbiased evidence from primary studies and improve the reliability of the results. This study addresses these gaps by employing a machine learning approach to automate the data extraction and mapping step, reducing errors and
effort, lowering the time required, gathering less biased evidence from primary studies, and improving the reliability of the resulting maps.

3.5 Data Collection and the Manually Annotated Baseline

The study employs secondary data in the form of full-text academic publications. The research corpus comprises the primary studies included in the Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD) systematic mapping study conducted by Binamungu and Maro (2023). The studies were obtained in PDF format from publishers' digital libraries and scholarly databases, including IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, and other relevant sources

The mapping study by Binamungu and Maro (2023) provides the manually annotated classifications used in this research. Specifically, Appendix A reports the classification assigned by the original authors to each of the 166 primary studies with respect to research type, contribution type, and evaluation method. The corresponding reference list maps each reference number to the title of the associated publication.

Following these

All 122 files correspond to primary studies included in the mapping study by Binamungu and Maro (2023) and were assigned the published manually annotated classifications. Text preprocessing prepares raw textual data for analysis. Full-text papers are first parsed from PDF into plain text with pdfplumber; a document whose pages contain no text layer (a scanned PDF) is passed page by page through the Tesseract optical-character-recognition engine instead. The abstract is located by a cascade of four strategies of decreasing strictness (a tightly delimited "Abstract" heading, a liberal look-ahead up to the next section heading, the text up to the first numbered heading, and finally the first 400 words of the body), so that every document yields a usable abstract. The reference list is stripped from the body so that cited titles do not contaminate

either the cue counts or the term statistics. Two views of each document are then kept: the whole body text without references, used by the facet assignment module and for TF–IDF features, and the title plus abstract, used for the sentence embeddings of the thematic component. Normalisation is deliberately light (lowercasing, tokenisation and English stop-word removal for the TF–IDF branch; no stemming), because the cue phrases and the transformer encoder both rely on natural surface forms.

Classifiers operate on numerical features, so text must first be represented as vectors. The Bag-of-Words model represents a document by term frequencies while ignoring word order, and Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF–IDF) weights each term by its frequency in the document relative to its rarity across the corpus, emphasising discriminative terms. These sparse representations are interpretable and effective for topic-bearing vocabulary, but they ignore context and treat synonyms as unrelated. Distributed embeddings address this by encoding words or sentences as dense vectors in a continuous space, so that semantically similar texts lie close together. Sentence-level embeddings, in particular, summarise an entire passage in a single vector and have been shown to support strong clustering and classification with relatively few labelled examples. The pipeline in this study combines TF–IDF with sentence embeddings so classifiers benefit from both discriminative surface terms and semantic context.

A small illustration clarifies how TF–IDF surfaces discriminative terms. In a corpus of mapping-study papers, a term such as “research” appears in almost every document and therefore carries a near-zero inverse-document-frequency, contributing little regardless of how often it occurs. A rarer, topic-bearing term such as “Gherkin” or “bubble plot” appears in few documents and so carries a high inverse-document-frequency; when it also appears several times in a given paper, its TF–IDF weight is large and it strongly characterises that paper. This is exactly the behaviour a facet classifier needs, because it amplifies the terms that distinguish one category from another and suppresses generic academic vocabulary. Its limitation is that it cannot see that “assessed in practice” and “evaluated through a case study” mean something similar is what the sentence embeddings compensate for, which is why the two representations are combined.

The study trains no model on human-annotated data. Facets are assigned without supervision, and thematic categories are induced without supervision, so model selection concerns the choice of representation, of algorithm and of hyperparameters rather than the fitting of a classifier to labelled examples.

Facets are assigned by comparison with natural-language descriptions of the published category definitions. Each category is characterised by a small set of anchor sentences composed from its definition. Anchors and documents are encoded by a single sentence-transformer model, and a document is assigned to the category whose closest anchor it most resembles. Because similarities are not comparable across categories, each category's scores are standardised across the corpus before comparison, which prevents a category whose description happens to resemble academic prose in general from absorbing the corpus. The separation between the winning category and the runner-up is retained as a measure of confidence.

The choice of text representation was settled empirically rather than assumed. Four representations were compared on the same corpus under the same clustering procedure: bag-of-words counts over unigrams and bigrams, term-frequency-inverse-document-frequency weighting, that weighting reduced by truncated singular value decomposition, and sentence-transformer embeddings. The comparison used criteria that require no labels, namely the silhouette coefficient, the Davies-Bouldin index and the topic coherence of the terms that characterise each resulting group.

Thematic categorisation proceeds by reducing the document embeddings with uniform manifold approximation and projection and clustering the reduced space. Two clustering algorithms are fitted so that the result does not rest upon a single procedure: k-means, whose number of clusters is selected by the silhouette coefficient over a sweep, and a density-based alternative which determines its own number of clusters and is permitted to leave documents unassigned. Descriptive terms for each group are obtained by class-based term-frequency-inverse-document-frequency weighting, so that a group is named by the terms that distinguish it rather than by the terms that are merely frequent within it.

Hyperparameters are selected by exhaustive grid search over the dimensionality of the reduction, the size of its neighbourhood and the number of clusters, scored by the silhouette coefficient together with topic coherence. Configurations that produce a group too small to interpret are excluded. The search is recorded in full so that the selected configuration can be seen in the context of those rejected.

Evaluation is constrained by the absence of a manually annotated reference set. No sample of studies was labelled independently by a human annotator against the category definitions, and in consequence accuracy, precision and recall against expert judgement cannot be computed at the level of the individual paper. The evaluation strategy is designed around that constraint and consists of four components, each of which is reported with an explicit statement of what it does and does not establish.

The first component is an internal audit of the facet assignments. A classifier is trained upon the assignments the pipeline itself produced and evaluated out of fold under stratified five-fold cross-validation, with the macro-averaged F1 score as the criterion so that rare categories weigh as heavily as common ones. This measures whether the assignments are recoverable from the text, which is a necessary condition for their being meaningful. It does not measure whether they are correct, and a category that cannot be recovered from its own assignments is treated as evidence that the category carries no signal.

The second component compares aggregate distributions with a published manual mapping of the same field. For each facet the share of studies the pipeline places in each category is compared with the published share, by the mean absolute error of the shares and by the correlation between the two share vectors. This is an indirect check: it can reveal a distribution whose shape is implausible, and it cannot confirm that any individual study is correctly placed. The reference corpus overlaps with but is not identical to the corpus analysed here, so exact correspondence would not be expected even from a perfect pipeline.

The third component evaluates the clustering by criteria that require no labels: the silhouette coefficient, the Davies-Bouldin index, the topic coherence of the descriptive terms, and the stability of the grouping under resampling, measured by the adjusted Rand index between clusterings fitted to overlapping subsamples. Stability is given weight alongside separation, on the reasoning that a grouping which does not survive the exchange of a fifth of the corpus is not a finding. The silhouette coefficient is interpreted with care, since its value depends upon the space in which it is computed and rises sharply under dimensionality reduction without the grouping itself improving.

The fourth component measures efficiency as the wall-clock time required to process the corpus, reported per study. This measurement is compared with published estimates of the time a human reviewer requires for the same task. The comparison is asymmetric, in that the automated figure is measured in this study while the manual figure is drawn from the literature, and it is reported as an indication of magnitude rather than as a controlled comparison.

A confidence signal accompanies every facet assignment, and its usefulness is itself evaluated. Since correctness cannot be established, the signal is tested against a computable proxy: whether the assignments it marks as uncertain are disproportionately those that the internal audit cannot recover. A signal that orders studies usefully is serviceable for directing human review even where its absolute reliability is unknown.

Development uses the Python programming language with established libraries: pdfplumber, pymupdf and pytesseract (with the Tesseract 5 engine) for PDF parsing and optical character recognition, pandas and NumPy for data handling, scikit-learn for TF–IDF features, the supervised classifiers, k-means and the evaluation metrics, umap-learn and hdbscan for dimensionality reduction and density-based clustering, sentence-transformers and BERTopic for the embeddings and topic descriptors, and Matplotlib for the visual maps. Ingestion, labelling, and evaluation run on an ordinary CPU environment; the transformer components run on Google Colab.

As the study relies on published primary studies rather than human participants, its principal ethical considerations concern the responsible use of copyrighted scholarly materials and the potential for model bias to result in unfair or misleading classifications. The full-text publications are used solely for research and analytical purposes and are not redistributed. All publications and data sources are appropriately acknowledged and referenced in accordance with established academic practices.

Potential biases in the automated classification models, particularly the risk of underrepresenting or inadequately classifying less frequently occurring facet categories, are systematically examined and transparently reported. To account for class imbalance and provide a more equitable assessment of model performance across categories, macro-averaged evaluation metrics are employed alongside other relevant performance measures. In addition, ethical and institutional approval for the research was obtained from the University of Dar es Salaam prior to data collection and analysis.

Non-functionally, it must be modular so that components can be replaced; reproducible so that runs are deterministic given the same inputs and seeds; transparent so that low-confidence decisions can be surfaced for human review; and efficient enough to process a study in a small fraction of the manual time. The preprocessing module prepares the extracted text for the three consumers described in Section 3.7. The labeller receives the whole body text without the reference list, lower-cased; the TF–IDF vectoriser receives the same text (or its first 3,000 words) and applies tokenisation, English stop-word removal and unigram-plus-bigram extraction; and the sentence encoder receives the raw title and abstract. No stemming is applied, because the cue phrases of the labeller and the transformer encoder both rely on natural surface forms. The module also computes the section-heading indicators of Section 3.8, which are shared by the labeller and the classifiers.

The facet assignment module allocates to each primary study a research type, a contribution type and an evaluation method. The module employs neither a keyword lexicon nor hand-crafted matching rules, and it is trained on no labelled data. Each category of each facet is instead characterised by three anchor sentences composed from its published definition. The research-type categories follow Wieringa et al. (2006); the contribution-type and evaluation-method categories follow Petersen et al. (2008). The complete set of anchor sentences is reproduced in the appendices.

Assignment proceeds by semantic similarity rather than by lexical matching. The anchor sentences and the text of each study are encoded by the same sentence-transformer model employed elsewhere in the pipeline, so that both inhabit a single vector space of 384 dimensions. The score of a study against a category is the cosine similarity to that category's closest anchor, that is, the maximum over the three anchors. Because categories are described rather than exemplified, a study may be assigned correctly even when its wording does not coincide with the definition, which constitutes the principal advantage of this approach over a lexicon.

Raw similarities are not comparable across categories. Certain anchor sentences lie closer to academic prose in general than others, and in consequence attract a disproportionate share of the corpus irrespective of content. Each category's scores are therefore standardised across the corpus before the maximum is taken, so that a study is assigned to the category it fits best relative to that category's typical fit. The magnitude of this correction is considerable: without it, the category Tool attracted 48 per cent of the corpus and the category Solution Proposal attracted a single study, whereas with it every category of every facet is populated. The correction is not, however, without cost, and its tendency to flatten the resulting distribution is examined below.

The textual evidence differs by facet, since the basis for each judgement resides in a different part of a paper. Research type is determined from the title and abstract; contribution type from the title, abstract and introduction; and evaluation method from the abstract together with the methodology and results sections.

Two quantities are recorded with every decision. The confidence is the cosine similarity to the winning anchor. The margin is the difference between the winning category and the runner-up, expressed in standard deviations of the standardised scores, and it is the more diagnostic of the two. A margin of zero denotes a tie between the leading categories, and a margin below 0.25 standard deviations denotes a decision in which the two leading categories are separated by less than a quarter of the typical spread of scores, and which should therefore be regarded as provisional. Studies falling below this threshold are flagged in a dedicated column for human review; the operation of that flag is evaluated among the results.

Transparency is achieved through the anchors rather than through matched phrases. A reviewer who disputes an assignment may consult the category description against which the study was matched, and the recorded margin states how narrowly the decision was reached. The anchors were composed from the published category definitions prior to any inspection of output and were not subsequently adjusted, so the procedure measures the extent to which an a-priori definition reproduces expert judgement rather than the extent to which definitions may be fitted to a known answer.

The pipeline is unsupervised throughout. No human-annotated labels are consumed at any stage, and no component is trained upon them. Supervised learning nevertheless occurs within the design, but as an instrument of measurement applied to the pipeline's own output rather than as a constituent of the pipeline itself. The distinction governs the interpretation of every figure the module produces and is therefore stated explicitly wherever those figures appear.

The module trains a classifier to predict each facet from the text of the study, using as targets the labels that the zero-shot module assigned, and evaluates it out of fold under stratified five-fold cross-validation. Stratification preserves the category proportions within each fold, which is necessary where categories are unequally populated. Three classifier families are compared by exhaustive grid search: logistic regression and a linear support vector machine, each across the regularisation parameter and with and without class balancing, together with a random forest across its depth, minimum leaf size and number of estimators. The selection criterion is the macro-averaged F1 score, under which each category contributes equally regardless of its frequency, so that a configuration cannot be rewarded for neglecting rare categories.

What this procedure measures is the internal consistency of the assigned label set, and not its correctness. A category that the zero-shot module applies coherently is recoverable from the text and attains a substantial F1 score; a category applied close to arbitrarily is not recoverable and attains a score approaching zero. The procedure thus constitutes an audit of the facet module, and a category whose F1 score is zero furnishes evidence that the category, as assigned, carries no signal. This outcome is observed and reported among the results.

The same instrument supports an ablation of the text representation, in which bag-of-words counts, term-frequency-inverse-document-frequency weighting, its dimensionality-reduced form and the sentence-transformer embedding are compared under a single classifier and a single cross-validation scheme. Holding the classifier and the evaluation protocol constant ensures that any difference observed is attributable to the representation.

It must be stated without qualification that the resulting figures do not constitute accuracy. The establishment of accuracy requires a manually annotated reference set, namely a sample of studies labelled independently by a human annotator against the same category definitions, and no such sample was available to the present study. The pipeline writes a pre-populated template for that exercise upon every execution so that it may be undertaken, and Section 6.5 records its absence as the principal limitation of the evaluation reported here.

The thematic module induces the topic-specific categories of the map directly from the corpus, using the embedding-based approach motivated in Section 2.4.6. The title and abstract of every study are embedded with the pre-trained Sentence-BERT model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dimensions); the embeddings are reduced with UMAP (cosine metric, minimum distance 0) and clustered with k-means. The number of clusters is not fixed in advance: k-means is fitted for k = 2 to 10 and for each UMAP setting of a small grid (2 or 5 components; 10, 15 or 30 neighbours), the

silhouette coefficient is computed for every solution, and the solution with the highest silhouette in the clustered space is retained (the silhouette method). A density-based HDBSCAN clustering is fitted on the same space for comparison, because it can flag outliers that fit no theme. Each cluster is labelled with its most characteristic terms by class-based TF–IDF, and the cluster-assignment confidence of a study is the relative margin between its distance to the nearest and to the second-nearest centroid. Topic diversity (the share of distinct terms among the cluster descriptors) and C_v coherence are reported alongside the silhouette so that the quality of the thematic structure is judged on more than one criterion.

The pipeline is implemented in Python 3.11 as one importable module organised in numbered sections (ingestion, labelling, manual-label handling and metrics, feature engineering and supervised classification, distribution benchmark, thematic module, orchestration) and driven by a Colab notebook that installs pinned dependencies, runs the whole study and generates the figures. This chapter presents and discusses the findings obtained when the pipeline described in Chapter Four was applied to the corpus described in Chapter Three. It first reports the experimental setup and the dataset, then the results of metadata extraction, of the definition-based facet labelling and of the supervised facet classification against the manually annotated reference set, the thematic modelling, the systematic map, the comparison with the manual baseline in both distribution and time, and the evaluation of the human-in-the-loop flag. The chapter then discusses the findings, considers the threats to validity, analyses the errors, and relates the results to the literature and to practice. Every number reported here is taken from the evaluation file of a single execution of the released pipeline; the figures are generated from the same file.

The primary-study folder contained 126 PDF documents, drawn from the behaviour-driven development mapping study of Binamungu and Maro (2023). No document was excluded on editorial grounds prior to analysis; the pipeline was applied to the folder as it stood, so that the reported yield reflects what an unattended run achieves.

Of the 126 documents, 123 were processed successfully, a yield of 97.6 per cent. The three that failed were examined individually and each was found to consist solely of page images with no text layer. Reading them requires optical character recognition, and the recognition engine was not installed on the machine employed. No document among the 123 that were processed required optical character recognition, so the text analysed throughout this chapter is the publishers' own.

The corpus so constructed comprises 1,242,356 words, with a median document length of 5,169 words and a range from 785 to 120,392 words. The upper extreme is not a paper: it is a complete conference proceedings volume. Ten documents exceed the length at which the interquartile rule regards a document as atypical, and Section 5.3 reports both their composition and a measurement of their influence on the results.

Two matters of scope must be stated before the results are read. First, this study possesses no manually annotated reference set. The per-paper classification published by Binamungu and Maro (2023) was not transcribed into a machine-readable form for this study, and no sample of studies was labelled independently by a human annotator. In consequence no comparison of per-paper decisions is possible anywhere in this chapter, and every figure reported is either a property of the pipeline's own output or a comparison of aggregate distributions. Second, and following from the first, the pipeline is unsupervised throughout: no component consumes a human label, and the supervised learning that appears in Sections 5.5 and 5.9 operates upon the pipeline's own assignments as an instrument of audit, in the sense established when the module was described.
5.3 Corpus Construction and Text Extraction Results

The corpus directory contained 126 PDF documents, of which the ingestion phase successfully processed 123, a yield of 97.6 per cent, producing a dataset of 1,242,356 words. The three documents that could not be processed were examined individually and found to contain no text layer whatsoever, consisting solely of page images. No PDF library is capable of reading such documents; optical character recognition would be required, and the recognition engine was unavailable on the machine employed. This limitation is carried forward to the discussion of limitations. None of the 123 documents that were processed required optical character recognition, so the extracted text is that of the publishers rather than a recognition of it.

One extraction defect was identified and corrected during development. It is reported here because it materially altered the results rather than merely the legibility of the text. In many publisher PDFs each word is stored as a separate typographic span carrying no space character, with the consequence that concatenating spans yields unreadable sequences in which an entire clause is joined into a single token. Forty-three of the 123 documents were affected, that is 35 per cent of the corpus. Prior to correction, the clustering procedure grouped the affected documents together and named the resulting group by fragments of publisher headers; following the insertion of a space wherever the horizontal separation between adjacent spans exceeds one fifth of the font size, no document remains affected and the clusters are named by research vocabulary. The episode illustrates concretely the contention that the quality of extraction bounds the validity of everything computed downstream.

Abstract recovery is reported according to the strategy that produced it, so that weaker rows may be audited rather than tacitly trusted. The abstract was located beneath its own heading for 105 studies (85.4 per cent), taken from the text preceding the introduction for 16 (13.0 per cent), and recovered by fallback for 2 (1.6 per cent). Titles were recovered from page typography for 115 studies, from the first line of text for 6 and from PDF metadata for 2. The publication year was recovered for 101 studies, spanning the interval 2010 to 2026, and author keywords for 56. The shortfall in keywords reflects the composition of the corpus, in which a substantial proportion of studies carry no keywords block.

Body sections were delimited by detecting headings from typography rather than from wording, on the grounds that headings are marked by size, weight and numbering rather than by vocabulary. Recovery varies by section, as the following table reports. Three refinements raised these figures during development: the incorporation of heading names actually employed by this corpus, among them Foundations, Preliminaries and Ontology Modelling, which a census of detected headings demonstrated were being left unmapped; the acceptance of compound headings such as Background and Related Work, which the original pattern rejected because it required the entire line to constitute a single section name; and the separate storage of the background section in place of its being subsumed within the introduction. Recovery of the methodology section rose from 31 studies to 56 in consequence, an improvement of 81 per cent.

Section recovery constitutes the weakest element of the ingestion phase, and its deficiencies propagate. The evaluation-method facet is determined from the abstract together with the methodology and results sections; for the 67 studies in which no methodology section was detected, that facet consequently rests upon less evidence than the design intends. This is a plausible contributor to its being the weakest of the three facets. All six body sections were recovered for only 12 studies.

Document length was examined for outliers prior to modelling, on the principle that a document substantially longer than a paper is frequently not a paper. Applying the interquartile rule, with quartiles of 3,557 and 8,559 words, yields an upper fence of 16,062 words. Ten studies exceed it, and these ten together account for 48.1 per cent of all text in the corpus; two are complete conference proceedings volumes rather than single studies. Their influence was measured rather than assumed. Their exclusion alters the cross-validated macro F1 by between 0.011 and 0.076 according to the facet, and alters the clustering of the studies that remain by an adjusted Rand index of 0.704, indicating that approximately 30 per cent of the grouping is contingent upon their presence. They are moreover assigned differently from the remainder of the corpus, half of them to Case Study against 17 per cent of the remainder, which suggests that the extraction misreads long documents systematically. The pipeline flags these studies and exposes a configuration setting by which they may be excluded. They were retained for the results reported here, and the argument for removing the proceedings volumes rests upon correctness rather than upon any improvement in the metrics.

The facet module assigned all three facets to each of the 123 studies. Since assignment is performed zero-shot, no training labels are withheld and no accuracy against a human answer may be reported. What can be reported is the distribution produced, the confidence with which each decision was reached, and the correspondence of that distribution with a published manual mapping of the same field. Section 5.5 subsequently audits the labels internally, and Section 6.5 records the absence of a manually annotated reference set as the principal limitation of this evaluation.

5.5 Internal Validation of the Assigned Labels

The assigned labels were audited internally by a procedure in which a classifier is trained upon the assigned labels and evaluated out of fold under stratified five-fold cross-validation. The question addressed is whether the assignments are recoverable from the text, which is a necessary condition for their being meaningful, and not whether they are correct.

Under grid search the best configuration attains a macro F1 of 0.513 for research type using a linear support vector machine, 0.484 for contribution type using logistic regression with class balancing, and 0.490 for evaluation method using logistic regression. Class balancing improves two of the three facets, which is consistent with the evenness of the distribution being an artefact of the assignment procedure rather than a property of the corpus. A random forest was inferior to both linear models on every facet, attaining between 0.348 and 0.404.

These aggregate figures conceal a division of greater consequence than the averages themselves. Of the fourteen studies assigned to Evaluation Research, a classifier trained upon those very assignments recovers none. The second is that a correlation computed over six category shares is a coarse instrument, and a high value establishes only that the ordering of categories is broadly reproduced. As already noted, the ordering is reproduced while the shape is not, the clearest discrepancy being the assignment of 14.6 per cent of studies to Opinion Papers against 0.5 per cent in the published mapping.

Felizardo et al. (2024) report a mean of 107 minutes per study for data extraction performed by a single reviewer, and 172 minutes where two reviewers extract independently and reconcile. This comparison must be read with an asymmetry in mind, and the asymmetry is material. The automated duration is a measurement taken in this study. The manual duration is an estimate drawn from the literature and was not measured here. The two quantities are therefore not commensurable in the way a controlled comparison would require, and the ratio between them should be treated as an order-of-magnitude indication rather than as a measured speed-up. A defensible efficiency claim would require timing a human reviewer extracting from a sample of these same studies, which remains future work.

A further qualification is that the two procedures do not produce the same artefact. The manual reviewer produces labels that have been read and judged; the pipeline produces labels that a human has not yet examined, of which between 27.6 and 36.6 per cent are flagged as provisional by the margin criterion. The time saved is therefore time saved on a first pass, not on a finished extraction, and the human effort required to review the flagged assignments is not included in the 46.4 seconds.

The facet module flags for human review every assignment whose margin falls below one quarter of a standard deviation, as defined when the module was described. The flag is intended to direct a reviewer's attention to the assignments least likely to be correct, and the question is whether it succeeds.

That question cannot be answered directly. Establishing whether a flagged assignment is wrong requires knowing what the right assignment is, which is precisely what a manually annotated reference set would supply and what this study lacks. An indirect test is nevertheless available and is reported here. If the margin carries genuine information about the reliability of an assignment, then assignments with a low margin should be disproportionately those that a classifier trained on the assignments cannot reproduce. Recoverability under cross-validation thus serves as a proxy for reliability: it is not correctness, but it is not independent of correctness either, since an assignment that no model can recover from the text is unlikely to reflect a property of the text.

Table 13 reports the test. On every facet, flagged assignments are recovered substantially less often than unflagged ones. The gap is 0.199 on research type, 0.220 on contribution type and 0.148 on evaluation method. The margin therefore carries real information, and a reviewer directed to the flagged studies would be examining the assignments the pipeline itself is least able to justify.
