The signal is real but weak, and the limits should be stated as plainly as the result. Even unflagged assignments are recovered only between 52.6 and 60.8 per cent of the time, so a reviewer who examined only the flagged studies would leave a substantial number of unreliable assignments unexamined. The correlation between the margin and recoverability is 0.231 on research type, 0.220 on contribution type and 0.087 on evaluation method, the last being weak enough that the flag should not be relied upon for that facet. Between 27.6 and 36.6 per cent of the corpus is flagged on each facet, which is a workable review burden but not a small one.

Two conclusions follow. The flag is defensible as a triage device, in that it orders studies usefully, but it is not a filter, in that clearing the unflagged studies is not safe. And the evaluation reported here is a proxy; establishing what the flag is worth in practice requires the manually annotated reference set whose absence is carried forward to the limitations.

The findings show that the data-extraction-and-mapping step of a software-engineering mapping study can be automated end to end to produce the artefacts a mapping study requires: a classified corpus, thematic clusters, a systematic map and a review list. They also show, when the output is measured against the published expert classification rather than against the pipeline's own labels, that per-paper facet classification is far from solved. Four observations stand out.

The map is reproduced; individual papers are not. The strongest result is the distributional agreement with Binamungu and Maro (2023) on the research-type and evaluation-method facets (benchmark scores 0.933 and 0.935, Table 11): the automated map has the right shape. The weakest result is the per-paper accuracy of 0.46 to 0.50 for the labeller (Table 7) and 0.43 to 0.57 for the supervised classifiers (Table 8), with macro-F1 between 0.33 and 0.41. The two findings are consistent: errors that cancel at the level of proportions still mislabel individual papers, and a mapping study needs both.

The imbalance is in the labels, not only in the corpus. The confusion matrix of Figure 9 shows the labeller sending 13 of the 40 validation-research papers to evaluation research and 13 to solution proposal, and assigning the tool category to twice as many papers as the experts (Table 14). These are not artefacts of an imbalanced training set but of category descriptions whose general wording ("case study", "framework", "system") fire in papers that merely mention them. The supervised classifiers, trained with balanced class weights on the manual labels, reduce the bias on the research-type facet (solution-proposal F1 0.69, validation-research F1 0.53) but cannot overcome the small number of
examples of the rare categories, which is why philosophical papers, metrics and rigorous analyses still reach an F1 of zero (Section 5.12).

Macro and micro reporting earn their place. Reporting both averages proved informative rather than ceremonial. The gap between them on every facet locates the residual weakness on the rare categories rather than letting a single accuracy figure conceal it, which is exactly the diagnostic the macro average exists to provide.

From labels to a map, with a human in the loop. The pipeline produced the SMS-specific outputs, the bubble plot, the thematic clusters and the review list, not just classification scores; this is the difference between a screening tool and a mapping tool, and it is the gap in the tool landscape (Tsou et al., 2020; Sundaram & Berleant, 2023) that this study set out to close. At the same time, Section 5.9 shows that the confidence signal orders studies usefully but is too weak to route human attention precisely. Taken together, the pipeline extends the proof-of-concept of Felizardo et al. (2024) into a complete, reproducible and manually annotated-evaluated system, and it addresses the three gaps of Section 2.6: a unified feature framework (Gap 1), a shared manually annotated reference set for heterogeneous mapping metadata (Gap 2), and an SMS-specific, software-engineering pipeline that produces evidence maps (Gap 3). It does so with strong distributional fidelity and with per-paper effectiveness that is reported without embellishment.

Interpreting the time saving. The measured 5.6 seconds per study is a saving of practically the entire manual cost, but it is a saving on the mechanical part of extraction only. Any realistic deployment keeps a reviewer in the loop, and the assisted-mode estimate of 74.6 minutes per study (30% saving) is the more honest planning figure; for a mapping study of a hundred or more primary studies it still compounds into several working days, which is the order of effort that prior surveys identified as the principal barrier to keeping maps current.

The threats to validity are discussed under the four headings customary in empirical software engineering: construct, internal and external validity, and reliability. For each, the threat, its likely effect on the results and the mitigation applied are stated.

Construct validity concerns whether the metrics measure what is intended. The main threat is that the reference classification is itself a human judgement whose reliability was not measured by its authors, so that some disagreements between pipeline and reference reflect the inherent ambiguity of adjacent categories rather than pipeline error. This is mitigated by using a peer-reviewed classification produced by two experienced researchers, by handling its multi-valued labels explicitly, and by reporting the confusion between adjacent categories as such in the error analysis. A second threat is that the distribution benchmark can be high while individual labels are wrong; it is therefore reported alongside, never instead of, the per-paper metrics.

Internal validity concerns whether the results follow from the method. The anchor sentences and the review threshold were fixed before any output was inspected, so the labeller's results cannot have been fitted to the test data. The supervised results are out-of-fold predictions under stratified cross-validation, and the configuration search is reported in full, with the stability of the selected configuration checked by repeated cross-validation; the best configurations differ from their neighbours by less than the standard deviation across repetitions, so the choice of winner is not decisive. The title matching that links PDFs to manual labels was checked by hand for every non-exact match.

External validity concerns generalisation. The corpus is anchored on a single behaviour-driven-development mapping study, which is topically homogeneous, reflected in the coarse thematic structure, so the findings, and especially the rare-category results, may not transfer unchanged to other domains. The anchor sentences were written for software-engineering facets and would need revision for another discipline; the supervised classifiers would need retraining. Validation on additional topics is left to future work.

Reliability concerns reproducibility. The modular, openly described pipeline, the fixed seeds and pinned versions, the released manual-label file and the single metrics file from which every number and figure is generated are intended to make the study reproducible by others; the thematic
component depends on a pre-trained model downloaded at run time, whose future versions could change the clusters, which is why the model name and version are recorded.

The per-class tables confirm the pattern implied by the distribution of the assigned categories. Categories announced by fixed phrases are recognised: rigorous analysis ("we prove", "formal verification") reaches an F1 of 0.67 from only 3 studies, and metrics 0.67 from 3. Categories that authors describe in many different ways are not: empirical insights (F1 0.05 for the labeller, 0.49 supervised), process contributions (0.17 and 0.37) and discussion (0.00 and 0.11). The practical reading is that the pipeline's assignments in the phrase-marked categories can be trusted with a light confirmatory glance, whereas the diffuse categories are exactly where a reviewer's attention is needed, which is the actionable detail that a single accuracy figure would conceal.

Errors cannot be enumerated in the ordinary sense, since establishing that an assignment is wrong requires knowing what is right, and no annotated corpus was available. What can be analysed are the failure modes the evidence exposes: categories that carry no recoverable signal, assignments the module itself cannot justify, and systematic distortions traceable to the ingestion of the documents. Four are identified, in order of the confidence with which they can be asserted.

The first and best-evidenced failure mode is category collapse. Several categories cannot be recovered from their own assignments by any classifier tested. On the research-type facet, Evaluation Research attains an F1 of exactly zero across fourteen assigned studies, and Opinion Papers attains 0.091 across eighteen. A category whose assignments no model can reproduce from the text is not encoding a property of the text, and the conclusion is that these categories, as assigned, are scatter. The failure is not one of the classifier but of the assignment: the anchor sentences for these categories evidently do not discriminate among the documents of this corpus.

The second is distributional distortion. The standardisation that prevents a single category from absorbing the corpus over-corrects, drawing the distribution towards uniformity. The discrepancy is quantifiable against the published manual mapping: 14.6 per cent of studies are placed in Opinion Papers against 0.5 per cent in the reference, and 17.9 per cent in Solution Proposal against 47.6 per cent. The direction of the error is consistent, in that categories the reference finds rare are over-populated and categories it finds common are under-populated, which is the signature of a procedure that equalises rather than one that misreads individual documents.

The third is the vocabulary gap, which persists in a different form from that which afflicts a keyword method. Because assignment proceeds by semantic similarity to a category description rather than by matching phrases, a study that states its contribution implicitly is no longer forced to a default category. It is instead assigned with a small margin, and between 27.6 and 36.6 per cent of studies fall below the review threshold on each facet. These are not failures to assign but assignments the module cannot justify, and the evidence that they are less reliable is direct: a classifier recovers flagged assignments substantially less often than unflagged ones on every facet.

The fourth is traceable to ingestion rather than to classification, and it is the most tractable. The evaluation-method facet is determined from the methodology and results sections, yet a methodology section was detected for only 56 of the 123 studies. That facet accordingly rests upon the abstract alone for much of the corpus, and it is the facet with the lowest median margin, the greatest number of flagged assignments and the weakest correlation between margin and recoverability. Document length compounds the problem: the ten longest documents, which together hold 48.1 per cent of the corpus text and include two complete proceedings volumes, are assigned to Case Study at three times the rate of the remainder, which indicates that long documents are being read systematically differently rather than merely noisily.

Taken together these modes suggest where effort would be repaid. Two of the four are properties of the assignment procedure and would be diagnosed directly by an annotated sample; the other two are properties of the ingestion and are addressable by improving heading detection and by excluding documents that are not single studies.

The pipeline can be situated against the prior work reviewed in Chapter Two. The proof-of-concept of Felizardo et al. (2024) reported that automated extraction with a large language model could approach manual quality for several facets while sharply reducing effort, with variability across data elements; the present study confirms both halves of that observation with a different technique and a full, published manually annotated reference set, finding near-total time savings and agreement that varies strongly with the category. Van Dinter et al. (2021) and Marshall and Wallace (2019) observed that automation in evidence synthesis has concentrated on screening, with extraction rarely evaluated end to end; the pipeline reported here is a direct response to that imbalance. Where Jonnalagadda et al. (2015) found that the absence of common manually annotated reference sets prevented comparison between extraction systems, this study shows that the classifications published in a mapping study can serve as such a standard at no annotation cost, which is a reusable methodological step. The design choice of linear classifiers with balanced class weights over sparse features is grounded in the text-classification literature (Allam et al., 2025), and the use of an embedding-and-clustering approach for the thematic component follows Weißer et al. (2020). Two cautions temper the comparison: the studies cited differ in corpora and facets, so their figures are not directly commensurable, and the present figures rest on a single anchored corpus.

For researchers conducting mapping studies, the results suggest a practical division of labour. The pipeline can shoulder the mechanical extraction, produce a draft map in minutes and record the evidence for every label, while reviewers confirm the labels, concentrating on the diffuse categories (empirical insights, process, discussion) and on the validation–evaluation boundary where the pipeline is least reliable. This is augmentation rather than automation, and the error analysis of Section 5.13 shows precisely where human attention pays off. For the discipline, the reproducible pipeline and the manual-labelled corpus lower the barrier to comparing automation methods and to keeping maps current. For institutions in low-resource settings, the modest

computational requirements of the ingestion, labelling and evaluation stages, which run on an ordinary computer, make adoption realistic; only the transformer components need a hosted environment such as Colab.

This chapter presents the conclusions drawn from the study, provides direct answers to the research questions, states the contributions of the work, acknowledges its limitations, and offers recommendations for future research and practice.

This study set out to design, develop and evaluate a machine learning pipeline for automating the data-extraction-and-mapping phase of systematic mapping studies, that phase being the costliest and least automated step of the systematic-mapping process. A modular pipeline was constructed which ingests full-text papers, recovers descriptive metadata and body structure, assigns each paper to the research-type, contribution-type and evaluation-method facets, induces thematic categories by means of transformer embeddings and clustering, and assembles a classified portfolio together with a visual map.

The pipeline is unsupervised throughout. No component consumes a human-annotated label at any stage. Facets are assigned zero-shot, by comparing each study with natural-language descriptions of the published category definitions rather than by matching keywords or by learning from examples. This is a stronger claim of independence from manual effort than the design originally envisaged, and it is also a weaker basis for asserting accuracy, since nothing in the design establishes that the assignments are correct.

Applied to 123 of the 126 primary studies of the behaviour-driven development mapping study of Binamungu and Maro (2023), the pipeline produced a complete systematic map in 46.4 seconds of wall-clock time. Its facet distributions correspond to the published manual mapping with benchmark scores of 0.938 on contribution type and 0.869 on both research type and evaluation method, the ordering of categories being broadly reproduced while the shape of the distribution is not.

Three findings are reported with confidence. First, semantic representation is decisively superior to lexical representation for this task: sentence embeddings surpass term-frequency weighting on every facet, and adding lexical features to semantic ones yields no improvement. Second, the quality of text extraction bounds everything computed downstream, a proposition demonstrated concretely when a space-loss defect affecting 35 per cent of the corpus caused the clustering to group documents by publisher rather than by subject. Third, the confidence margin carries real information about which assignments the pipeline can least justify, and is therefore serviceable as a triage device for human review.

Two findings are reported as limitations rather than as results. The facet distributions are implausibly even, an artefact of the standardisation the assignment procedure requires; and several categories cannot be recovered from their own assignments by any classifier, which indicates that those categories, as assigned, carry no signal. Both are consequences of assigning facets without supervision, and both would be measurable, and possibly correctable, against a manually annotated reference set.

The principal conclusion is therefore qualified. The data-extraction-and-mapping phase can be automated end to end without supervision, and the resulting map is produced in seconds rather than in the hundreds of hours a manual extraction requires. Whether the map is correct remains unestablished, and establishing it is the first item of future work.
Research Question 1: Which unified set of publication-metadata features can be used to extract and map data in a systematic mapping study?

The study defined a unified feature set organised into two groups: descriptive bibliographic metadata (title, abstract, length, page count and, from the reference record, venue and year) and analytical map-defining facets (research type, contribution type, evaluation method and thematic category), with the category sets of the reference mapping study, as set out in Table 2. Treating these as one connected framework, with the same document representation feeding every facet, answered the first question and addressed the absence of a unified extraction framework.
Research Question 2: How can a manually annotated dataset of full-text academic papers be collected, preprocessed and annotated to train and validate the models?

A corpus of 122 full-text software-engineering papers on behaviour-driven development was assembled from the primary studies of Binamungu and Maro (2023), and its manual labels were obtained without new annotation by transcribing the per-paper classification published in that study and matching it to the files by title. Three views of each document were prepared: the whole body for the labeller, TF–IDF with cue and section features for the classifiers, and the title and abstract for the sentence encoder. The approach, reusing the classification of a published mapping study as ground truth, is itself reusable for any field with a manually conducted map.
Research Question 3: How can an end-to-end machine learning pipeline be designed and implemented to automate SMS data extraction, facet classification and thematic mapping?

The pipeline was implemented as one sectioned Python module for ingestion (with OCR fallback), preprocessing, facet assignment with confidence and evidence, supervised classification trained on the manual labels, thematic modelling with the number of clusters chosen by the silhouette method, and map generation, driven by a notebook that also produces every figure. The modular design, described in Chapter Four, made each component independently testable and upgradeable and produced the SMS-specific outputs that distinguish a mapping tool from a screening tool.
Research Question 4: What is the performance of the pipeline compared with the manual approach?

The pipeline produces, for all 122 studies, the same kinds of output a manual mapping study produces, so it is functionally equivalent in output. On quality, at the level of the map it reproduced the manual facet distributions with benchmark scores of 0.933, 0.858 and 0.935; at the level of individual papers its labels agreed with the experts for 45.9% to 49.6% of the studies (supervised: 43.4% to 57.4%), well below expert consistency, with the rare and diffusely described categories the main source of error. On effort, it needed 5.6 seconds per study against 107 minutes manually, or an estimated 75 minutes when flagged studies are re-checked by a reviewer. The answer, then, is that the pipeline matches the manual approach well in the aggregate map and in speed, and not yet in the classification of individual papers.

The study makes four contributions. First, it provides a unified feature framework that links publication metadata to the established mapping facets, closing the gap left by tools that address only isolated fields. Second, it delivers a manually annotated dataset of 122 behaviour-driven-development studies with per-paper labels for three facets, derived from a peer-reviewed mapping study, together with the method for deriving such datasets from any published map; this supports reproducible benchmarking where shared manually annotated reference sets were previously absent. Third, it contributes a complete, reproducible, end-to-end pipeline that performs extraction, facet labelling and classification and thematic mapping and produces evidence maps, extending the proof-of-concept of Felizardo et al. (2024) into a full system with an OCR fallback, evidence-bearing labels and a review flag. Fourth, it provides an honest, manually annotated evaluation of that pipeline, distinguishing what automation already does well (the aggregate map, the mechanical extraction) from what it does not (rare and diffuse categories, targeting of human review), which is the evidence base the field needs to decide where to invest next.
The limitations of this study are stated here in order of the severity with which they constrain the conclusions that may be drawn.

The absence of a manually annotated reference set is the principal limitation. No sample of studies was labelled independently by a human annotator against the category definitions, and in consequence the accuracy of the facet assignment is unknown. The figures reported for the internal audit measure the internal consistency of the assigned labels, that is, the degree to which a classifier can recover them from the text, and they do not measure correctness. Objective four of this study, which requires evaluation against a manually curated baseline, is therefore only partially met: the comparison of distributions provides an indirect external check, whereas the direct comparison it envisages remains outstanding. The pipeline writes a pre-populated template for the labelling exercise upon every execution, and the exercise is the first item of future work.

The assignment procedure flattens the facet distributions. The standardisation described in Section 4.6 was introduced to prevent a single category absorbing the corpus, and it succeeds in that respect, but it draws the distribution towards uniformity. The comparison with the manual baseline with the published mapping shows the resulting shape to be implausible in at least one respect, namely the assignment of 14.6 per cent of studies to Opinion Papers against 0.5 per cent in the published mapping. The category shares reported in this study should accordingly not be interpreted as estimates of the composition of the literature.

Section recovery is incomplete and its deficiencies propagate. A methodology section was detected for 56 of the 123 studies and a discussion section for 42. Since the evaluation method facet is determined from the methodology and results sections, that facet rests upon less evidence than the design intends for a substantial part of the corpus, and it is indeed the facet with the lowest median confidence margin and the greatest number of studies flagged for review.

The corpus is small and confined to a single research area. One hundred and twenty-three studies of behaviour-driven development is sufficient to demonstrate a pipeline but not to establish that its behaviour generalises to other fields, to larger corpora, or to literatures whose publication conventions differ. The silhouette values reported are low throughout, which is the expected consequence of a corpus concentrated upon a single topic and should not be read as a defect of the clustering algorithms.

Three studies could not be processed. Each consists solely of page images with no text layer, and the optical character recognition engine required to read them was not available on the machine employed. The reported results therefore rest upon 123 of the 126 studies in the corpus, a yield of 97.6 per cent.

Ten studies exceed the length at which a document ceases to resemble a single paper, and two of these are complete conference proceedings volumes. Together the ten account for 48.1 per cent of the text in the corpus. Their influence was measured rather than assumed, as reported above, and they were retained for the results presented here; a study that excluded them would be defensible and would yield somewhat different figures.

Finally, the comparison of processing time contrasts a measured quantity with a published estimate. The automated duration was measured on the machine used throughout. The manual duration is drawn from the literature and was not measured in this study, and the comparison should be read with that asymmetry in mind.

Building on these results, five directions are recommended. First, the corpus should be extended to mapping studies in other domains and topics, using the same method of transcribing published classifications, to test external validity and to give the rare categories enough examples to learn. Second, the rarer and diffusely described categories should be strengthened: position-aware cues (weighting phrases in the abstract, introduction and evaluation sections above those in related work), anchor sentences refined against an annotated sample, sentence embeddings and fine-tuned transformer classifiers, and class-imbalance remedies such as oversampling, all with the multi-label metrics of this study. Third, the confidence signal should be improved by combining the labeller's margin with the probabilities of the supervised classifiers and re-evaluated as in Section 5.9, so that the human-in-the-loop mode routes attention where it is needed. Fourth, the thematic module should be run with the silhouette-selected k-means configuration on the full corpus and its clusters aligned with the manual themes of the reference study. Fifth, a usable interface should be developed so that researchers without programming expertise can apply the pipeline and maintain living maps.

Two further avenues deserve attention. The pipeline currently begins after study selection; integrating it with the screening-automation tools reviewed in Chapter Two would yield an end-to-end system from search results to finished map. In addition, the emergence of large language models for extraction, illustrated by Felizardo et al. (2024), suggests a hybrid design in which a language model proposes candidate facet labels that the lighter, auditable labeller and classifiers verify; such a design could combine the recall of generative models with the transparency and
reproducibility that evidence synthesis requires, and the manually annotated dataset of this study is the benchmark on which it could be tested.

The findings carry practical recommendations for several groups. For researchers conducting mapping studies, the pipeline is best adopted in its assisted mode, with the automated facet labels treated as a first pass that a reviewer confirms with the help of the stored cue evidence, so that the time savings of Chapter Five are realised without ceding final judgement; the codebook in Appendix IV provides a ready basis for consistent checking. For tool builders, the modular architecture of Chapter Four shows that descriptive metadata extraction, analytical facet classification and thematic discovery should be treated as separate components with separate quality targets, because each has a different error profile and a different appropriate technique. For the wider software-engineering research community, the study demonstrates that the classifications published in mapping studies can be turned into shared manually annotated datasets at no annotation cost, and it offers the dataset and configuration described here as a contribution toward that shared infrastructure. For supervisors and research-training programmes, the transparent, auditable design demonstrates that automation can be introduced into evidence synthesis without compromising the methodological rigour that examiners expect.

Systematic mapping studies remain expensive because the extraction and mapping of data from full-text papers is performed by hand. This study has shown that the phase can be automated end to end without any labelled training data, and that a complete map of 123 primary studies can be produced in under a minute on an ordinary machine.

The contribution is a reproducible unsupervised pipeline rather than a validated classifier, and the distinction matters. What has been demonstrated is feasibility: that full-text papers can be ingested, structured, assigned to published mapping facets by semantic comparison with category definitions, grouped into themes, and rendered as a map, with every intermediate artefact written to disk and every decision accompanied by a confidence margin. What has not been demonstrated is accuracy, because no human-labelled sample was available against which the assignments could be scored.

The evaluation reported for the evaluation is accordingly an audit of the pipeline's internal consistency and of the correspondence between its aggregate output and a published manual map. That evaluation is informative, and it was candid in identifying categories that carry no signal and a distribution whose shape is not credible. It is not, however, a substitute for comparison with expert judgement, and the present work should be read as establishing a method and an infrastructure upon which such a comparison can now be conducted at modest cost.

The wider implication is that the obstacle to automating this phase is no longer representational. Semantic embeddings capture enough of what a paper is about to group it and to compare it with a category definition. The obstacles that remain are the fidelity of text extraction from publisher PDFs, which this study found to govern every downstream result, and the availability of annotated samples against which automated judgement can be calibrated. Neither is a problem of machine learning, and both are tractable.

The following condensed definitions, adapted from Wieringa et al. (2006) and Petersen et al. A study is a solution proposal when it proposes a novel technique and argues for its relevance with a small example; validation research when the technique is investigated in a laboratory or controlled setting; evaluation research when the technique is implemented and evaluated in practice; an experience paper when it reports the authors' experience; a philosophical paper when it offers a conceptual framework or taxonomy; and an opinion paper when it states a position. Contribution type is assigned by the principal artefact or knowledge delivered: tool, method, process, model, metric or empirical insights. Evaluation method records the strongest form of evaluation present: example, case study, experiment, experience report, discussion, rigorous analysis or simulation. The reference study assigns more than one category where a paper warrants it.

The terms below are used throughout the dissertation with the specific meanings given here, to remove ambiguity between everyday and technical senses.
Operational definition as used in this study

A secondary study that classifies a body of primary literature along predefined facets to reveal publication trends, clusters and gaps, as distinct from a systematic literature review, which synthesises findings to answer a focused question.
The phase of an SMS in which structured information is recovered from each primary study and used to position it within the map; the phase this study automates.
One of the predefined classification dimensions of a mapping study; here, research type, contribution type and evaluation method.
The descriptive and analytical attributes of a paper, such as venue, year, research type and contribution type, that populate the map.
The per-paper classification published in a manually conducted mapping study, treated as ground truth for evaluating the pipeline and for training the supervised classifiers.
The component that assigns a facet category by counting weighted cue phrases, with a confidence equal to the margin between the best and second-best category.
The unweighted mean of the per-class F1-scores, used as the primary effectiveness measure because it treats rare and common categories equally.
An F1-score computed by pooling decisions across all classes, reflecting overall instance-level performance and dominated by common categories.
One minus the mean absolute difference between the pipeline's and the reference's share of each category of a facet.
An operating mode in which facets labelled below a confidence threshold are routed to a human reviewer rather than being accepted automatically.
The integrated sequence of modules (ingestion, preprocessing, labelling, classification, thematic modelling and map generation) that together automate the extraction-and-mapping phase.
